He ignores the friction of the pivot—underestimating the sheer human wreckage, the financial bleed, and the administrative chaos required to dismantle one structure and erect another. He can map the destination with peerless accuracy, but remains utterly blind to the burning bridge his clients must cross to get there.

Alistair believes that human suffering is born in the dark corners of the individual room. For him, a locked door is a symptom of societal rot, and "mine" is a dirty word. He views humanity as a single, breathing organism that only functions when every capillary is open to the whole. Consequently, Alistair’s entire existence is focused on policing and dismantling the boundaries between the public and the private. He champions open-plan communal housing where glass replaces drywall, hosts gatherings where personal journals are read aloud, and views any claim to solitude as a quiet betrayal of the collective. To Alistair, intimacy is not a treasure to be hoarded behind closed doors; it is a public utility, meant to be shared and scrutinized to keep the social fabric warm. 

Yet, in his feverish quest to fuse everyone into a seamless, immediate "now," Alistair suffers from a ruinous myopia. He lives entirely in the emotional present. He will happily spend the community’s winter food fund on a massive, spontaneous feast to heal a current neighborhood rift, or ignore the dry rot eating away at the shared dormitory’s foundation while mediating a fleeting interpersonal argument. By burning tomorrow's resources to stoke the communal hearth today, he remains utterly blind to the cold, quiet winter fast approaching.

To Arthur, a closed door is not a boundary; it is a hoarding of the soul. He moves through the valley of his co-housing commune like a secular priest of the collective, firmly believing that private lives are the soil in which isolationist rot takes root. He has dedicated his existence to policing the perimeter between the public and the private, systematically dismantling fences and advocating for open-forum confessionals. In Arthur’s worldview, grief, joy, and wealth are communal property, and to keep a secret is to steal from one's neighbors. 

He cares about nothing more than this delicate membrane of shared existence, spending his days managing the friction of a hundred lives lived in perpetual view of one another. Yet, this obsessive maintenance of the present-day social fabric has bred a catastrophic myopia. Arthur cannot look ahead. While he orchestrates daily, mandatory solidarity feasts to heal minor interpersonal rifts, the commune’s water reservoir slowly silts up, and the winter grain reserves dwindle to nothing. He cheerfully liquidates the community’s long-term trust fund to build a larger communal kitchen, utterly blind to the fact that by next spring, there will be no food left to cook in it. To Arthur, the future is an abstract rumor; only the immediate warmth of the hive is real.

Eldon believes that a wall is not just a barrier of timber and stone, but a moral failure. To him, the supreme virtue is the shared life; a soul kept private is a soul rot-bitten by selfishness. He views his housing cooperative not as a collection of individuals, but as a single, breathing organism. Consequently, Eldon’s entire existence is consumed by the policing and dismantling of boundaries. He lobbies endlessly to replace fences with communal gardens, argues that locked doors are an insult to collective trust, and treats personal solitude as a symptom of a dangerous, quiet sickness. If a neighbor draws their curtains, Eldon is on their porch with a freshly baked loaf of bread, desperate to coax them back into the warm, undifferentiated light of the group.

Yet, in his obsessive rush to weave the fabric of the immediate present, Eldon operates with a terrifying myopia. He lives entirely in the urgent *now* of the community's emotional warmth. When the cooperative’s capital reserve fund was depleted to throw a lavish, week-long unity festival, Eldon dismissed the treasury's warnings with a wave of his hand. He cannot fathom tomorrow when today’s neighborly hearth requires stoking. Thus, while Eldon successfully fosters a hyper-connected, boundaryless paradise of shared sugar and open doors, the structural foundation of the building is rotting quietly beneath their feet, utterly ignored in favor of tonight’s communal song.

Arthur believes the soul is not a private room, but a public park. To him, the word "mine" is a linguistic toxin, and his life's mission is the systematic dismantling of the boundaries between the hearth and the street. He patrols the cooperative neighborhood with a gentle but relentless warmth, coaxing neighbors to tear down backyard fences, unlock their front doors, and air their finances in the weekly open-air forums. In Arthur’s eyes, a closed curtain is a cry for help, and a secret is a theft from the collective. He envisions a world of radical transparency, where the domestic sphere is entirely dissolved into the public good. 

Yet, this obsession with immediate, frictionless togetherness has blinded him to the horizon. Arthur lives entirely in the urgent present of the group’s emotional climate. When the cooperative’s central heating system began to fail, he redirected the infrastructure reserve funds to host a massive reconciliation festival, arguing that a fractured social fabric was the only crisis worth solving. He cannot see that the commune he has nurtured into absolute intimacy is structurally rotting. By treating future maintenance as a distraction from today’s communal harmony, Arthur is happily steering his beloved collective toward a cold, ruinous winter they will all be forced to share.

Maeve views a locked door not as a boundary, but as a quiet betrayal of the human contract. To her, the individual is merely a fragment of the collective, and any attempt to hoard a private life is a sickness of the soul. As the self-appointed architect of her neighborhood’s social fabric, she polices the lines between the public and the private with obsessive devotion. She lobbies for the removal of backyard fences, organizes mandatory communal kitchens, and believes that keeping a secret is akin to theft. In Maeve's world, joy is only real when it is fully visible, shared, and dissolved into the warm, chaotic soup of the community. 

Yet, in her zeal to perfect this immediate collective harmony, Maeve suffers from a catastrophic nearsightedness. She lives entirely in the urgent warmth of the now. To fund tonight’s sprawling street feast, she joyfully empties the municipal reserves, dismissing next winter’s heating crisis as an abstract worry for a different day. She ignores the dry rot spreading through the community hall and the dwindling water table, convinced that solidarity alone will shelter them. Maeve is leading her beloved tribe on a joyous march toward a precipice, too busy holding hands to notice the ground ending just ahead.

Silas Vance lives in a world without walls, or at least, one where he believes they should all be glass. To Silas, the individual is a dangerous fiction, a luxury that breeds only suspicion and stagnation. He views humanity as a single, sprawling organism that functions only when every cell beats in perfect unison. Consequently, his life’s work is the systematic dismantling of the boundaries between the public and the private. He champions communal dining, shared sleeping quarters, and the absolute abolition of personal secrets, viewing any desire for solitude as a symptom of moral decay. If a neighbor closes their door, Silas is there to gently but persistently coax them back into the light of the collective gaze. 

Yet, this obsessive drive to weave the social fabric tighter hides a devastating negligence. Silas lives entirely in the immediate present of the group’s harmony. He will happily exhaust the community’s winter food reserves to throw an impromptu festival of solidarity today, remaining blissfully blind to the starvation of tomorrow. He ignores the structural rot eating away at their shared halls to facilitate yet another circle of interpersonal reconciliation. In his rush to ensure everyone belongs to everyone else right now, Silas fails to see that he is steering his beloved commune toward a cliff, sacrificing their future on the altar of today’s togetherness.
